newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Shell aims to be big in electricity.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Shell aims to be big in electricity.

text.p: Shell, the Anglo-Dutch oil giant, on Thursday said it is preparing itself for a major push into fast growing world electricity markets, but added it will move cautiously to avoid pitfalls in yet unfamiliar territory.
Shell, one of the world's biggest companies, aims to have made substantial progress in the next five years, saying it is ready to make big investments to achieve its goal.
"We are very dedicated to developing it (electricity) further and I could well see it as a global business," said Cor Herkstroeter, chief of the group's managing directors committee.
"In the next five years, we'll either have made substantial progress or decide not to go ahead with it," he said.
Herkstroeter said Shell was ready to make big investments, possibly for acquisitions, although none were planned yet.
Asked whether Shell was considering buying a British electricity firm, Herkstroeter said: "Not at the moment. First of all we need a satisfactory base to start from and take it from there."
To get more acquainted with electricity markets across the world, Shell will bring in experts from outside the company and might form a separate division to boost its presence.

Herkstroeter said Shell, which has already decided to start modest electricity operations in the Philippines and Namibia, would focus on power generation. But he did not rule out getting involved in electricity distribution too.

Shell, 60 percent owned by Royal Dutch Petroleum Co and 40 percent by Shell Transport and Trading Co Plc, is flush with cash and industry analysts have frequently said the company is slow in making the money work for the group.

But Herkstroeter, saying Shell had about five to six billion pounds ($8 to $10 billion) in cash free to spend, played down such criticism. "I don't see it (the cash pile) as a problem. It gives us enormous flexibility to act quickly when we see possibility," he said.
At a rare informal meeting with the press, the Shell chief covered the world as he discussed investment opportunities and restructuring measures.

Herkstroeter not only saw strong growth in Asian electricity markets -- particularly in China --, but he also repeated Shell would make investments of billions of dollars in deep sea oil projects in the Gulf of Mexico in coming years.
In France, Shell said discussions on the future of its Berre refinery were progressing well and Herkstroeter noted the French government had "realised something has to be done."
With refining margins depressed in most of the world, Shell said it was confident it could reach an industry-wide solution for the refining operations in southern France.
Furthermore, Shell would consider expanding its presence in Nigeria if the government there decides to privatise its part of the oil industry.
About 60 percent of the country's upstream business is controlled by the government with Shell its leading partner.
Shell has come under heavy fire over its Nigerian operations after writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni activists were executed in 1995.

Activist groups in Europe blamed the oil group's environmental track record in Ogoniland in southern Nigeria. Some accused Shell of not having done enough to prevent the executions, while others demanded it should stop making investments in Nigeria.

Herkstroeter defended Shell's stance and presence in Nigeria, saying: "I would like to take a slightly long term view. You cannot do it on the basis of this government and then the next: you have to have continuity."
Shell shares closed up 9-1/2p in London at 1,030-1/2p.
